Bataan Death March. Following the fall of the Bataan Peninsula in the Philippines in April nineteen forty-two, Japanese forces conducted a brutal forced march of American and Filipino prisoners of war. Approximately six thousand to ten thousand soldiers died from starvation, disease, and brutal treatment, making it one of the most notorious war crimes of the Pacific campaign and a symbol of Japanese brutality.

The campaign occurred from January to April nineteen forty-two on the Bataan Peninsula near Manila. An American garrison under General Edward King surrendered on April ninth, nineteen forty-two. Approximately seventy-six thousand American and Filipino troops surrendered, and Japanese forces under General Masaharu Homma began a forced march toward prison camps.

The prisoners marched one hundred four kilometers over six days in tropical heat with minimal food, water, and medical care. Japanese soldiers killed stragglers and those too weak to continue. The death toll was estimated at six thousand Americans and fifteen thousand Filipinos, though Japanese military refused to acknowledge the atrocity for decades. Survivors testified to systematic beatings, executions, disease, and starvation, while physicians were prevented from administering medical care.

The brutality did not go unpunished. General Homma was executed for war crimes in nineteen forty-six, and several of his subordinates were also tried and convicted. The event galvanized American hatred of Japan and determination to defeat them, fulfilling General Douglas MacArthur's vow to return to liberate the Philippines, which would ultimately happen at the Battle of Leyte Gulf.
